n: The heading ties this psalm to David fleeing from his son Absalom’s rebellion. David cries out: Lord, so many enemies are rising up against me!

f.w: many are they that rise up against me

n: Many say God won’t rescue him. “Selah” is a pause marker — perhaps a musical interlude or a moment to reflect.

f.w: There is no help for him in God

f.g: A Hebrew term of uncertain meaning, probably a musical or liturgical pause.

n: But David turns to God: you are my shield, my glory, and the one who lifts my head when it hangs in shame.

f.w: the lifter up of mine head
f.g: The one who restores dignity and hope.

n: He cried aloud to the Lord, and God answered him from his holy mountain.

f.g: Mount Zion, where the ark of the covenant was kept.

n: Even surrounded by danger, David lay down, slept, and woke again, because the Lord held him up. Peaceful sleep is evidence of trust.

f.w: I laid me down and slept

n: He will not fear even tens of thousands of enemies surrounding him.
David prays, “Rise up, Lord, and save me!” Striking an enemy on the jaw and breaking his teeth means making him powerless to bite.

f.g: An old battle cry used when the ark set out.

f.w: broken the teeth of the ungodly

n: Salvation belongs to the Lord alone. David ends not with his own needs but with a blessing on all God’s people.
